topic_summary: Analysis of the Renaissance humanist project to reconstruct Classical Latin from ancient texts, examining the tension between medieval Latin as a living, drifted vernacular and humanist Latin as a recovered textual form. The core question is whether the reconstructed classical form was reachable through continuous evolution from medieval drift or constituted a discontinuous reoccupation of a separate kernel accessed only through textual symbols.

key_entities: Medieval Latin (living vernacular with Germanic borrowings, Vulgate influence, palatalization drift)
Classical Latin (textual form from Cicero/Virgil, no living speakers post-antiquity)
Lorenzo Valla (philologist, Elegantiae linguae Latinae 1441-49, descriptive approach)
Ciceronian Movement (Bembo, Sadoleto, prescriptive imitation, papal authority)
Erasmus (Ciceronianus 1528, critique of servile imitation, vocabulary crisis)
Humanist minuscule (orthographic purification for international publication)
key_tensions: Living drift vs textual recovery (medieval users vs humanist reconstructors)
Prescriptive vs descriptive philology (Ciceronians vs Valla)
Orthographic purity vs vernacular pronunciation (published vs handwritten Latin)
Lexical adequacy vs stylistic purity (Erasmus vs strict Ciceronians)
key_mechanisms: Ad fontes methodology (textual criticism to recover ancient forms)
Papal authority enforcement (Rome as center of Ciceronian orthodoxy)
Minuscule standardization (orthographic purification in published works)
key_absences: Phonological reconstruction evidence (how did humanists pronounce reconstructed Latin?)
Non-elite literacy practices (did reconstruction penetrate beyond scholarly circles?)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The Latin language as authoritative medium for scholarship, law, theology, and international communication
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Textual authority grounded in ancient manuscripts (Cicero, Virgil, Quintilian) vs living practice authority grounded in continuous institutional use

readings.commitment: Correct Latin is the form actually used by competent speakers/writers in continuous institutional practice, incorporating natural linguistic evolution
readings.authority_grounding: Living practice, institutional continuity, vernacular influence as legitimate evolution
readings.expected_structural_delta: Low suppression of innovation; vocabulary expands with need; pronunciation follows vernacular; orthography reflects speech; beneficiary: practicing scholars/clerics; victim: textual purists

readings.commitment: Correct Latin is the form used by ancient authors (especially Cicero), recovered through philological analysis of manuscripts, excluding post-classical drift
readings.authority_grounding: Textual authority of golden age authors, philological method, papal/humanist institutional power
readings.expected_structural_delta: High suppression of medieval forms; vocabulary frozen to classical corpus; orthography purified; pronunciation uncertain; beneficiary: humanist elite; victim: medieval scholastic tradition, functional communication

readings.commitment: Correct Latin balances classical models with functional adequacy for contemporary needs, allowing neologism when ancient vocabulary is insufficient
readings.authority_grounding: Pragmatic synthesis (Erasmus, Valla's descriptive method), functional communication needs
readings.expected_structural_delta: Moderate suppression; classical style preferred but not absolute; vocabulary innovation permitted for new concepts; beneficiary: working scholars in law/medicine/science; victim: strict Ciceronians, linguistic orthodoxy

axiom_contradictions.basis: Living drift treats continuous use as constitutive of correctness (language is what competent speakers do); textual recovery treats ancient texts as normative regardless of living practice (language is what the texts say). No single framework can hold both: either living practice or textual authority is the ultimate arbiter of correctness.

omegas.description: Was classical Latin recovery reachable from medieval drift or a discontinuous reoccupation? Evidence suggests both: genealogical continuity (same language family, shared institutions) yet epistemological discontinuity (recovered through philology, not living practice). The 'symbol' (classical text) became the kernel, displacing living drift.
omegas.source: User's kernel contest formulation + research context showing humanist Latin as 'development of medieval Latin' yet claiming 'radical rupture'

omegas.description: How did humanists pronounce reconstructed Latin? Orthographic purification occurred without phonological reconstruction methodology. Likely continued vernacular pronunciation despite classical spelling, creating a split between written and spoken forms.

Did humanist reconstruction penetrate beyond scholarly elites? Evidence shows papal/humanist institutional backing, but unclear whether lower-level clerics, notaries, or provincial scholars adopted classical standards or continued medieval practice.
omegas.source: Absence inventory (§1.1) + beneficiary/victim analysis showing humanist_elite vs functional_communication split

omegas.description: Do the three readings genuinely instantiate different constraints or collapse into one? Living_drift and textual_recovery hold contradictory axioms (practice vs text as authority). Hybrid_adequacy may be a compromise position rather than a third constraint, but Erasmus/Valla's descriptive method suggests distinct structural delta (functional adequacy as independent criterion).

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel/reading decomposition applied per §1.3-K. Three readings selected capture the structural contest: living drift (medieval practice), textual recovery (humanist reconstruction), hybrid adequacy (Erasmian synthesis). Axiom contradiction declared between living_drift and textual_recovery (practice vs text as ultimate authority). Hybrid_adequacy may be compromise rather than third constraint; omega_reading_collapse_risk documents this uncertainty.
